title: LRU and LFU caches
idea: An LRU or LFU cache is a fixed-size key-value store that, when full, evicts the least recently used or least frequently used entry.

analogy.text: Your desk holds three open books. To open a fourth, you shelve the one you have not touched for the longest. That is LRU.
analogy.breaks: The desk does not count how often each book was used, which LFU needs.

points: A cache stores values by key and evicts one entry when it is full.
The eviction rule is a strategy: `LRUPolicy` or `LFUPolicy` behind one interface.
LRU drops the key unused for the longest time; LFU drops the least-used key.
A JavaScript `Map` keeps insertion order, so it can double as a recency list.

hero.title: An LRU cache of size three

steps.caption: `put('A')` adds A at the newest end. The cache has room for three keys.
`put('B')` joins behind A. Order means recency, not value.
`put('C')` fills the cache. A is now the oldest key.
`get('A')` is a hit. A moves to the newest end, so B becomes the oldest.
`put('D')` finds the cache full. The oldest key, B, is evicted before D goes in.
`get('B')` is a miss. The caller must load B from the slow source again.
At step five, LFU counts uses instead: A has two, B and C one each. The tie goes to the older key, B.

code.title: Map as a recency list
code.caption: Delete and set again to move a key to the newest end. Remove the read of `a` and run: a different key goes.

code.title: Cache with pluggable eviction
code.caption: One `Cache` class, two policies, the same calls. Write a `FIFOPolicy` whose `touch` records a key only the first time, and pass it in.

walk.text: The policy interface: record a use, forget a key, and name the next victim.
LRU: `touch` moves the key to the end, so the first key is the victim.
LFU: count uses. Re-inserting keeps ties ordered by recency.
The victim is the lowest count; the first such key wins ties.
`Cache` owns the data and receives its policy, so it never knows the rule.
Evict only when a new key arrives and the cache is full.
A has three uses (one put, two gets); B has one. LRU drops A; LFU drops B.

pitfalls: Calling `set` on an existing `Map` key does not refresh its recency; delete it first.
Check capacity only for new keys, or updating a value evicts an entry for nothing.
This `LFUPolicy` scans every key to evict; use frequency buckets when O(1) matters.

quiz.why: Setting an existing key updates its value in place. A `Map` keeps the key's original position, so `x` stays first.

takeaway: Store data in one place and make the eviction rule a swappable policy.

starters: How do I build an O(1) LFU cache with frequency buckets?
